Name: language_agnostic_reasoning_core
Title: Do LLMs Reason in a Language-Agnostic Latent Space? A Circuit-Level Test
Short Hypothesis: We hypothesize that multi-step reasoning in multilingual LLMs is carried by a language-agnostic subspace in the residual stream: the same features and heads perform a reasoning step regardless of the input/output language, while language identity is factored into a separable subspace that is only re-applied at detokenization. This is the best setting because it directly separates 'linguistic form' from 'reasoning content' at the mechanism level, which behavioral cross-lingual benchmarks cannot do; a simpler correlational probe cannot establish that the SAME circuit is reused.
Related Work: Prior work shows cross-lingual transfer (Conneau et al.) and that multilingual models pivot through English-like representations (Wendler et al. 2024, 'Do Llamas work in English?'). Mahowald et al. (2024) argue for a formal/functional competence split conceptually. Feng et al. and Bricken et al. (SAE) give tools for feature extraction. We go beyond correlational 'shared representation' claims by causally testing feature and head reuse across languages on matched reasoning tasks via activation patching and cross-lingual SAE feature alignment, distinguishing 'reasoning core reuse' from 'English pivoting'.
Abstract: Whether large language models reason in a language-independent 'mentalese' or merely translate to a dominant language and reason there remains unresolved and is central to understanding the link between language and machine intelligence. We test the language-agnostic reasoning core hypothesis mechanistically. Using matched multi-step arithmetic-word-problem and logical-entailment items translated into 6 typologically diverse languages, we (i) train sparse autoencoders on the residual stream and align features across languages via activation-correlation matching, (ii) apply cross-lingual activation patching, transplanting the mid-network state of a reasoning step from a source-language run into a target-language run, and (iii) locate reasoning-critical heads via path patching and test whether the same head set is causal across languages. We predict that a stable set of mid-layer features/heads implements each reasoning operation identically across languages, that patching a reasoning-step state cross-lingually preserves the correct answer, and that language-identity features are concentrated in early and late layers. We contrast this with the English-pivot account, which predicts target-language runs converge onto English-token feature geometry. Results would show whether 'intelligence' (reasoning) is architecturally dissociable from 'language' (surface form), quantify how much of reasoning is language-bound, and identify the layers where the transition from form to content and back occurs. This clarifies whether scaling language modeling yields genuinely amodal computation or language-tethered heuristics.
Experiments: Build a matched dataset: 300 GSM8K-style arithmetic word problems and 300 logical-entailment items, human-translated into English, Chinese, Arabic, Swahili, Hindi, Finnish; verify answer invariance.
Run Llama-3-8B/70B and Qwen2.5 on all items; record per-token residual streams at every layer.

Train per-language SAEs (or one shared SAE) on residual streams; align features across languages by maximizing activation-correlation on aligned reasoning tokens; report alignment score and fraction of 'universal' features.

Cross-lingual activation patching: take the residual state at the layer/token where a reasoning step completes in language A and paste into the corresponding position in language B; measure answer-preservation rate vs same-language patching baseline.
Path patching / head attribution: identify heads whose ablation drops reasoning accuracy; compute Jaccard overlap of causal-head sets across languages.
Layerwise language-identity probe: linear probe for input language at each layer; predict high accuracy early/late, low in mid reasoning layers.
Metrics: cross-lingual patch answer-preservation rate, causal-head Jaccard overlap, feature-alignment AUC, layerwise language-probe accuracy curve.
Control: patch with a random unrelated state (should destroy performance) and patch within-language (upper bound).
Risk Factors and Limitations: SAE feature alignment across languages may be underdetermined; correlation-based matching can create spurious pairs.
Tokenization differences mean 'corresponding positions' for patching are approximate; may bias results.
Findings could be model-family specific and not generalize to models with weaker multilingual coverage.
Distinguishing 'language-agnostic core' from 'strong English pivot that low-resource languages also route through' requires careful controls and may be partially confounded.
Translation artifacts could make some items easier/harder, confounding accuracy comparisons.
